title: Compound Interest Explained: Same $96K, 2.4x the Money
description:
Two people each invest $96,000. One ends up with about $494,000, the other about $203,000. The difference is compound interest, and it comes down to four numbers: how much you put in, the rate, time, and the leaks (fees, inflation and taxes). We work through each one with simple examples, the Rule of 72, the real cost of a 1% fee, and nominal vs real returns.

Assumptions: all returns are illustrations, not forecasts. 7% a year before fees unless stated (other rates shown for comparison), monthly contributions at the end of each month, 3% yearly inflation, fees modelled as a reduction in the yearly return, no taxes in the examples. Real investments go up and down and can lose money. Tax-advantaged account rules vary by country.

Source: S&P 500 total return in 2008 (-36.55%, dividends included): Damodaran, NYU Stern, Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills: https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/histretSP.html

For education only. Not financial advice.

scenes.say: Two friends each invest ninety-six thousand dollars. Same investment, same returns. At sixty-five, one has about two hundred thousand dollars. The other has almost half a million.
Maya puts in two hundred dollars a month, starting at twenty-five. Sam waits until forty-five, then puts in four hundred a month to catch up. Both put in exactly ninety-six thousand dollars.
Sam saved twice as hard, yet Maya ends up with almost two and a half times as much money. Same dollars in. The only difference was when they went in.
That gap is compound interest, and it comes down to just four numbers. By the end of this video, you'll know how each one works, and which one people underestimate the most.
First, what compounding actually is.
Say you invest ten thousand dollars, and it earns seven percent a year. That rate is just an assumption for this video, not a promise. After one year, you've earned seven hundred dollars.

Here's the key. In year two, you earn seven percent on ten thousand seven hundred, not just on ten thousand. So you make seven hundred and forty-nine dollars. That extra forty-nine is interest on your interest.
It looks tiny. But each year's growth joins the pile, and the bigger pile earns more. By year thirty, you're earning almost five thousand dollars in a single year, without adding a cent.
This is the compounding loop. Your money earns a return. The return is added to your balance. A bigger balance earns a bigger return. And it repeats, every single year.

Compare that with simple interest, where you only ever earn on the original ten thousand. After thirty years, simple interest gets you thirty-one thousand dollars. Compounding gets you about seventy-six thousand.
Same starting money, same seven percent, and more than double the result, simply because the growth was allowed to grow.

visual.text:
Your money earns money.
Then that money
earns money too.

scenes.say: You can write the whole thing in one line. What you end up with depends on how much you put in, the rate it grows at, how long it grows, and what leaks out along the way. Those are the four levers.

visual.title: The whole idea in one line

lines.text: where Rate is what's left after fees, taxes and inflation

scenes.say: Lever one: how much you put in.
Most people don't invest one big lump. They invest a bit every month. So let's switch to a monthly example: three hundred dollars a month, for thirty years, at the same assumed seven percent.
You'd put in one hundred and eight thousand dollars of your own money. At the end, you'd have about three hundred and fifty thousand.
That means about seventy percent of the final pile is growth. Your own contributions are the smaller slice.

This lever is the simplest, because it's a straight line. Double what you put in, and you double what you end up with. One hundred a month becomes about one hundred and seventeen thousand. Five hundred a month becomes about five hundred and eighty-five thousand.
Small increases add up too. If you raise that three hundred by three percent every year as your income grows, you'd end with about four hundred and eighty thousand instead of three hundred and fifty.
So the lesson for lever one: you don't need a big amount to start. But whatever you add over time goes straight into the machine.

visual.title: Lever 1 in a nutshell
items: Twice the money in = twice the money out
Raise it when your income rises

scenes.say: Lever two: the rate of return.

Keep everything the same, three hundred a month for thirty years, and only change the rate. At three percent, you end with about one hundred and seventy-four thousand. At five, about two hundred and forty-five thousand. At seven, three hundred and fifty-one thousand. And at nine, over half a million.

visual.title: $300 a month for 30 years, at different rates

scenes.say: Notice that's not a straight line. Going from seven to nine percent adds about one hundred and sixty thousand dollars. Two percentage points, and the result grows by almost half.
So naturally, people chase higher rates. This is where it gets risky. Higher expected returns almost always come with bigger swings. Investments that can rise faster can also fall harder.

visual.text:
Higher returns
come with
bigger swings.

scenes.say: For example, in two thousand and eight, the S and P five hundred, a basket of five hundred large US companies, lost over a third of its value in a single year, even including dividends.

visual.label: S&P 500 in 2008
visual.sub: total return incl. dividends · source in description

scenes.say: And losses hurt more than gains help. If an investment rises fifty percent and then falls fifty percent, the average return is zero. But your ten thousand dollars has turned into seven thousand five hundred.

So a bumpy ride grows slower than its average suggests. Up forty percent, then down twenty, again and again, averages ten percent a year. But your money only grows about five point eight percent a year. Less than a steady seven.

visual.title: What you actually keep each year

scenes.say: And be very careful with anyone promising high returns with little or no risk. Guaranteed big returns, pressure to act fast, profits that never dip. Those are classic warning signs of a scam.

visual.title: Red flags
items: Can't explain how it makes money

scenes.say: We're not here to tell you what to invest in. The lesson for lever two is simple: a slightly better rate is powerful, but a too-good-to-be-true rate is a trap.
Lever three: time. This is the one people underestimate the most.
There's a handy shortcut called the Rule of seventy-two. Divide seventy-two by your yearly return, and you get roughly how many years it takes your money to double.
At three percent, money doubles about every twenty-four years. At seven percent, about every ten. At nine percent, about every eight.

So at seven percent, ten thousand dollars invested at twenty-five roughly doubles every decade. About twenty thousand by thirty-five, thirty-nine thousand by forty-five, seventy-six thousand by fifty-five, and almost one hundred and fifty thousand by sixty-five.
Now look at where the growth happens. The last decade adds more than the first three decades combined. Those final years are the most powerful, and you only get them if you start early.

Back to monthly investing: three hundred dollars a month until sixty-five. Start at twenty-five, and you end with about seven hundred and forty thousand. Start at thirty-five, about three hundred and fifty thousand. Start at forty-five, about one hundred and fifty thousand.

Waiting ten years, from twenty-five to thirty-five, saves you only thirty-six thousand dollars in contributions. But it cuts your ending balance by more than half. That's nearly four hundred thousand dollars.

visual.title: The cost of waiting ten years

scenes.say: Remember Maya? Her first ten years of deposits, just twenty-four thousand dollars, end up as more than half of her final balance.

visual.title: Maya's balance at 65

rows.label: From her first 10 years of deposits ($24,000)

visual.note: $200 a month from 25 to 35, left to grow at an assumed 7%

scenes.say: That's the real power of time. Your earliest dollars are the most valuable dollars you'll ever invest, because they get the most doublings.

visual.text:
Your earliest dollars
get the most
doublings.

scenes.say: Lever four: the leaks. Fees, inflation, and taxes.
Fees first. A fund fee of one percent a year sounds tiny. But it's charged on your whole balance, every year, so it compounds against you.

visual.label: a year in fees sounds tiny
visual.sub: but it's charged on your whole balance, every year

scenes.say: Back to three hundred a month for thirty years. With no fees, about three hundred and fifty-one thousand. With a zero point one percent fee, about three hundred and forty-four thousand. With one percent, about two hundred and ninety-two thousand. And with two percent, just two hundred and forty-five thousand.

visual.title: $300 a month for 30 years, assumed 7% before fees

scenes.say: So a one percent fee quietly takes about one sixth of your final balance. That's almost sixty thousand dollars, for a fee that sounded like nothing.

Next, inflation. Prices rise over time, so a future dollar buys less than a dollar today. At three percent inflation, prices roughly double every twenty-four years. That's the Rule of seventy-two again.

So the three hundred and fifty-one thousand you'd have in thirty years would only buy what about one hundred and forty-five thousand buys today. That's the difference between nominal returns, the number on your statement, and real returns, what the money can actually buy.

Taxes are the third leak. Many countries offer accounts where investments can grow without being taxed every year, like retirement accounts in the US, ISAs in the UK, or tax-free savings accounts in Canada. Rules differ, so check what applies to you.

visual.title: Tax-advantaged accounts (examples)
items: Rules and limits vary by country

scenes.say: Now put the leaks together. An assumed seven percent return, minus a one percent fee, minus three percent inflation, leaves a real return of roughly three percent a year.

visual.title: From headline return to real return

scenes.say: So which lever matters most? Let's line them up.
Our base case: three hundred a month for thirty years, at seven percent, with no fees, ends at about three hundred and fifty-one thousand. Now let's change just one thing at a time.

visual.label: our base case
visual.sub: $300 a month · 30 years · assumed 7% · no fees

scenes.say: Starting ten years earlier gets you about seven hundred and forty thousand. Doubling the monthly amount, about seven hundred thousand. Two extra points of return, about five hundred and ten thousand. And a one percent fee pulls it down to two hundred and ninety-two.

visual.title: Change one thing from the base case

scenes.say: Time wins, and look at the cost. The ten extra years add just thirty-six thousand dollars of contributions. Doubling the amount adds one hundred and eight thousand. Yet the extra years still produce the bigger result.
Here's the catch. The amount, you can raise slowly. The leaks, you can shrink. The rate is partly risk and partly luck. But time is the only lever that disappears if you don't use it.
So what does this mean for you?
One: start as early as you can, even if the amount feels too small to matter. Small and early beat big and late, just like Maya and Sam.
Two: automate it. Set up a monthly transfer so investing happens before you can spend the money, and raise it whenever your income goes up.
Three: watch the costs. Check what fees you're paying, because a one percent difference can cost tens of thousands of dollars over a lifetime.

visual.label: what a 1% fee cost in our example
visual.sub: $300 a month · 30 years · assumed 7% before fees

scenes.say: Four: think in real terms. Ask what your money will buy, not just how big the number looks. And stay skeptical of any promise of high, guaranteed returns.

visual.text:
Ask what it will buy,
not how big it looks.

scenes.say: So, the four numbers that decide your wealth: how much you put in, the rate you earn, how long you give it, and how much leaks out. Of those four, time is the one you can never get back.

lines.text: Time is the one you can't get back.

scenes.say: If this made compounding click, subscribe. We explain how money really works, every week. And tell us in the comments: which lever surprised you most?
